page: Amazon Web Services c7i-flex.large is an x86_64 cloud server instance built on the AWS Nitro Hypervisor. It features a 3.2 GHz Intel Xeon 8488C processor provisioned with 1 physical core supporting hyperthreading for 2 virtual CPUs (vCPUs). The CPU allocation is designated as burstable. The processor incorporates 48 KB L1 data cache, 2 MB L2 cache, and 105 MB L3 cache, alongside specialized instruction sets including AVX-512 and AMX extensions for matrix operations. It is equipped with 4.0 GB of DDR5 system memory operating at 5 GHz, providing a RAM-to-vCPU ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU. The instance includes no local NVMe storage, zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses, and no GPU hardware accelerators.

Benchmark measurements indicate a distinct asymmetry between single-threaded and multi-core performance for the c7i-flex.large. Single-threaded metrics are strong, with a Geekbench single-core score of 2067.0 and a single-threaded Gzip compression throughput of 33.49 GB/sec. However, multi-core performance tests yield lower relative outputs, including a multi-core stress-ng rating of 2086.47 and a Geekbench multi-core score of 2547.0. Memory throughput tests show uncached read and write speeds of 13.13 GB/sec and 14.34 GB/sec, resulting in a PassMark memory score of 866.04. Redis SET operations reach 2.42 million operations per second, while static web serving throughput measures 4.08 GB/sec. Small 135M parameter LLM inference processing registers 284.83 prompt tokens per second and 61.45 generation tokens per second.

The hardware profile offers cost efficiency for lightweight or periodic computational tasks that leverage single-threaded clock speed without requiring sustained multi-core saturation. The 1:2 RAM-to-vCPU ratio combined with DDR5 memory supports low-memory entry-level application runtimes. However, sustained multi-threaded workloads, intensive memory-bound computations, and large database operations face bottlenecks due to burstable CPU limits, lower memory throughput, and the absence of local ephemeral storage. Primary workload fits include lightweight single-threaded microservices, entry-level web serving, periodic batch scripts, and basic text parsing tasks.
